subject: zoology
question_text: Mention the advantages of some UV rays to us.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.60, VSAQ 152). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Killing microbes
lines: UV rays kill the micro organisms present on
This keeps the skin surface free of harmful
steps.why: The question asks for advantages in the plural, so two separate uses are needed; this is the first and it is the one students forget because UV is usually taught as a harm.
common_mistakes: Writing only about the harmful effects of UV. The question asks for the ADVANTAGES.
Writing that UV kills germs inside the body. It acts on the body SURFACE.
steps.memory_tip: Two uses, two places: on the skin it kills microbes, in the skin it makes vitamin D.
steps.margin_note: One short sentence per advantage. Do not write about ozone here.

steps.label: Vitamin D

lines.text: UV rays make vitamin D in the skin

lines: UV rays convert the sterols present in the
Vitamin D is needed for the absorption of
calcium and so for strong bones.
steps.why: Naming the starting material, the sterols, is what separates a full answer from the half answer that only says sunlight gives vitamin D.
common_mistakes: Writing that UV rays contain vitamin D. They CONVERT the sterols in the skin into it.
Leaving out the word sterols, which is the named material in this step.
steps.memory_tip: Sterols in the skin plus UV gives vitamin D; vitamin D then brings in the calcium.
steps.margin_note: Name the sterols and the vitamin. One extra line on what the vitamin does.

insider_note: This is a two-point question and each point is a separate mark, so a student who writes four lines on vitamin D alone still scores only one.
